passage:
The Durga Puja committee hall in Salt Lake was packed, and Uma's father had introduced her to eleven people in twenty minutes. "My daughter. Cleared the civil services. All-India rank 212!"

Uma smiled at every aunty and uncle. Inside, her stomach turned. Training hadn't even started. She might hate it. She might not be good at it.

When a neighbour asked, "So when will you be a collector?", Uma found her father by the bhog counter.

"Baba," she said quietly, "I love that you're proud. Really. But it's only the beginning. Things can go wrong. I don't want you telling everyone I'm going to be a collector."

Arnab's face fell a little. "I'm just happy."

"I know. I'm happy too." She squeezed his arm. "Would you still be proud if I ended up in a small posting, doing ordinary work?"

He looked at her properly. "Uma, I was proud when you learned to ride a cycle."

She laughed, and her stomach finally settled.

qa.q: What rank did Arnab tell people Uma got?
qa.a: All-India rank 212.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling as her father introduced her to everyone?
qa.a: She felt warm at his pride but pressured and anxious, since training hadn't started and things could go wrong.

qa.q: What did Uma do well in talking to her father?
qa.a: She thanked him for his pride, set honest expectations that success could change, and asked whether his love depended on the title.

qa.q: How does Arnab see his daughter's success?
qa.a: Arnab is simply happy and proud, and his pride in her goes back to her learning to ride a cycle, not just the rank.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman whose father boasts about her success, feeling warm and pressured, and setting honest expectations while checking his love does not depend on the title.

passage:
Dear Tejas,

You're the only person I can say this to. Mummy and Papa have told every relative, every neighbour, even the vegetable vendor that I'm a "senior engineer at a big American company." Papa printed my offer letter and framed it. Mummy's phone status is a photo of my office badge.

I'm touched, bhai. I really am. After everything they spent on my studies, I understand.

But I'm on a six-month probation. Two people in my team were let go last month. If that happens to me, I don't know how Papa will face the colony.

This weekend I'm going to tell them, gently, that I'm happy they're proud, but that jobs like this aren't permanent. I'll ask Mummy to take down the badge photo. And I'll tell Papa I need to know they'll love me the same if things change.

Wish me luck.

Your brother,
Mohit

qa.q: What did Papa do with Mohit's offer letter?
qa.a: He printed it and framed it.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling about his parents' boasting?
qa.a: Mohit felt touched by their pride but anxious and pressured, fearing what would happen if he lost the job on probation.

qa.q: What does Mohit plan to tell his parents, and why is it wise?
qa.a: That he's glad they're proud but the job isn't permanent, asking Mummy to take down the photo and asking Papa for reassurance that their love won't change, which sets honest expectations.

qa.q: How might Papa feel hearing Mohit's worry?
qa.a: Papa may feel surprised and a little embarrassed, but also moved that Mohit worries about his feelings.

grounding: The letter shows a young man whose family boasts about his job, feeling warm and pressured, and planning to set honest expectations so their love does not depend on the title.

passage:
Ulla's first novel had hit the bestseller list in Sweden, and suddenly everyone in Gothenburg wanted to have coffee with her.

A former classmate who'd ignored her for years sent flowers, then asked if Ulla could introduce her to Ulla's publisher. An old neighbour praised her "genius" and asked for free copies for his whole book club. A stranger at a party called her "the voice of a generation" and then pitched his own manuscript.

Ulla enjoyed it, at first. Then she noticed the pattern. Praise, then a favour.

She met Kaito, her friend from the bakery job she'd had at twenty-two, who'd read every bad draft.

"Everyone loves me now," she said, half joking.

"I loved the chapter with the grandmother," Kaito said. "The ending's weak, though."

Ulla laughed with relief. "Thank you for saying that."

She sent polite thank-yous to the flatterers and politely declined most of the favours. Kaito she invited to the launch.

qa.q: What job did Ulla and Kaito share at twenty-two?
qa.a: A bakery job.

qa.q: What did Ulla feel when Kaito said the ending was weak?
qa.a: She felt relieved and grateful to hear honest criticism from someone who had been there before her success.

qa.q: How did Ulla handle the sudden flattery?
qa.a: She noticed the pattern of praise before favours, thanked people politely, declined most requests, and kept close to her truthful friend.

qa.q: How does Kaito see Ulla's success?
qa.a: Kaito is happy for her but still treats her the same, giving honest feedback as a real friend would.

grounding: The passage shows someone suddenly praised and asked for favours after success, noticing the pattern, checking who was there before, and valuing a friend who tells the truth.

passage:
Two weeks after Jeevan was made head of procurement at the Mangaluru hospital, his desk was covered in boxes of sweets. Vendors who had never returned his calls now called him "sir" and praised his "vision." A senior doctor who had ignored him for a year invited him to lunch, then asked him to fast-track an order for a particular brand of equipment.

Jeevan felt flattered, then uneasy.

At the canteen he sat with Irawati, the store-room supervisor who had trained him when he joined.

"Everybody suddenly thinks I'm brilliant," he said.

"You're not," Irawati said, dipping her vada in chutney. "You're decent. And you still forget to check expiry dates."

He burst out laughing. "Thank you."

That afternoon, he returned the sweets with polite notes, told the senior doctor the order would go through the normal process, and asked Irawati to keep telling him when he was wrong.

qa.q: What did the senior doctor ask Jeevan to do?
qa.a: Fast-track an order for a particular brand of equipment.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as the sweets and praise piled up?
qa.a: He felt flattered at first, then uneasy about the pattern of praise and favours.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do to protect himself from the flattery?
qa.a: He returned the sweets politely, kept the order in the normal process, and asked Irawati to keep telling him when he was wrong.

qa.q: How does Irawati see Jeevan's promotion?
qa.a: Irawati sees him as decent, not brilliant, and treats him the same, which makes her a truthful friend.

grounding: The passage shows someone suddenly praised and asked for favours after a promotion, noticing the pattern and keeping a truthful friend who tells him when he is wrong.

Jasleen: WHAT 🎉🎉 I told you!!

passage:
Preeti was the first woman agriculture officer the block office near Satara had ever had. On her first day, farmers lined up to ask her about soil tests, seed subsidies and a strange fungus on their grapes.

She answered what she could. Inside, a voice kept whispering: they'll find out you only topped the exam. You've never grown anything.

That evening, her colleague Aditi found her staring at a pile of files. "Tired?"

"Scared," Preeti admitted. "I feel like a fraud. The farmers know more than me."

Aditi laughed gently. "They know their fields. You know the science. And everyone feels like this in their first year. I did."

"So what do I do?"

"Keep a notebook of what you get right. When you don't know, say so and find out. And spend a day on a farm every week. Learn from them."

The next morning, Preeti told a farmer, "I don't know that fungus yet. I'll ask the university and come to your field on Thursday." He nodded, satisfied.

qa.q: What was strange on the farmers' grapes?
qa.a: A fungus.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling as she stared at the files?
qa.a: She felt scared and like a fraud, worried the farmers knew more than her.

qa.q: What did Aditi suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping a notebook of successes, admitting when she doesn't know and finding out, and learning on farms weekly, which builds real skill without pretending.

qa.q: How might the farmer see Preeti's honest answer?
qa.a: The farmer seems satisfied and may trust her more because she promised to find out rather than guessing.

grounding: The passage shows a young officer feeling like an impostor after success, learning many feel this, keeping a record, admitting what she doesn't know and continuing to learn.

passage:
I'm Sudha. Last March my small design agency in Pune lost the biggest bid of our year, a new hospital's whole signage system, to Pixelworks, the agency across the road.

I was furious. At the office I called them "copy-paste merchants." At a networking lunch, I nearly said worse to a client. My business partner, Madhuri, kicked my ankle under the table.

That evening she asked, "What did they do better?"

I didn't want to answer. Then I did. I called the hospital's procurement officer and politely asked for feedback. She told me: their price was a bit lower, but mainly they'd visited the site three times and brought patient feedback. We'd sent a beautiful PDF and never visited.

That stung more than losing.

We changed how we pitch. Now we visit every site at least twice before bidding. We won the next two hospital contracts. And I never bad-mouthed Pixelworks again. I'd only made myself look small.

qa.q: What did the rival agency do that Sudha's didn't?
qa.a: They visited the site three times and brought patient feedback.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling after losing the bid?
qa.a: Sudha felt furious and envious, calling the rival "copy-paste merchants."

qa.q: What did Sudha do instead of continuing to sneer?
qa.a: Sudha asked the hospital for feedback, learned what the rival did better, and changed the agency's pitching by visiting sites before bidding.

qa.q: How might the client at the networking lunch have seen Sudha bad-mouthing a rival?
qa.a: The client may have seen it as unprofessional and petty, which could have hurt Sudha's credibility.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone envious after losing a bid, choosing to ask what the rival did better and improve, and learning that sneering harms their own credibility.

passage:
Sales head's note, Monday

Chinmay, our youngest account manager, lost the textile-mill contract on Friday to a rival supplier. I watched how he handled it today.

At the morning meeting he was bitter. He said the rival "must have bribed someone" and started drafting a post for an industry group about their "cheap quality." I asked him to hold the post for a day.

We sat together. I asked, "What did they offer that we didn't?" He didn't know. So he called the mill's purchase manager, politely, and asked. The answer: faster delivery and a named contact who answered calls on Sundays.

Chinmay was quiet after that. "So they just served them better."

He deleted the draft post himself. He has proposed a weekend support rota for our three biggest clients, and asked to visit the rival's public trade stall next month to learn how they present.

I am proud of how he turned that around.

Kiran, sales head

qa.q: What did the rival offer that Chinmay's company didn't?
qa.a: Faster delivery and a named contact who answered calls on Sundays.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling at the morning meeting?
qa.a: He felt bitter and envious, accusing the rival of bribery and wanting to post about their quality.

qa.q: What did Kiran help Chinmay do instead?
qa.a: Kiran asked him to hold the post, and helped him find out what the rival did better so he could improve with a support rota.

qa.q: How might the rival supplier have been affected if Chinmay had posted?
qa.a: The rival could have been falsely accused in public, and Chinmay's own company could have lost credibility.

grounding: A sales head's note shows a young manager envious after losing a contract, learning what the rival did better and improving instead of bad-mouthing them.

passage:
At the monthly review in the Coimbatore office of Kamal's pump company, the same name came up again: Rajni Engineering, the rival across the highway. They'd delivered forty irrigation pumps to the cooperative two days early, again.

Some of the senior staff grumbled. "They must be cutting corners."

Kamal shook his head. "I checked. They're not. They're just good. Their after-sales team visits farms within a day."

Rajni, the young engineer on Kamal's own team, raised her hand. "So what can we learn?"

"Their service schedule, for one," Kamal said. "We could visit farms faster too."

Rajni added, "And the cooperative wants solar pumps next year. Neither of us can make both kinds fast enough. Maybe we could bid for different parts of the order?"

The room went quiet. Then the general manager said, "Draft it."

Kamal walked out smiling. Respecting the rival hadn't meant giving up. It had given them a plan.

qa.q: How many pumps did the rival deliver early?
qa.a: Forty irrigation pumps.

qa.q: What did Kamal feel about the rival company?
qa.a: Kamal felt respect and admiration for their consistently good delivery, and was curious about what to learn.

qa.q: What ideas came out of respecting the rival?
qa.a: Learning from their fast service schedule and possibly collaborating on different parts of the solar pump order.

qa.q: How do the senior staff see the rival at first?
qa.a: They suspect the rival must be cutting corners, unwilling to believe the rival is simply good.

grounding: The passage shows someone admitting a rival consistently delivers well, learning from them, and seeing where collaboration could serve both without giving up.

passage:
Dear Ms. Lakshmi,

We haven't met, though our firms have competed for school uniform contracts in Madurai for three years. I'll be honest: your team has beaten us four times, and every time I studied your work, I understood why. Your stitching holds up, and the schools say your delivery is always on time.

I'm writing with an idea. The district has just announced a uniform order for 180 schools. Neither of our firms can produce that alone by June. If we bid together, you on shirts, us on skirts and trousers, where we're strongest, we could both deliver well.

I'm not giving up competing with you on other contracts. But on this one, our interests seem to align.

Would you be open to a meeting next week? I'm happy to come to your unit.

With respect,
Ritu Selvam
Ritu Garments

qa.q: How many schools were in the district's uniform order?
qa.a: 180 schools.

qa.q: What does Ritu feel about Lakshmi's firm, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ritu feels real respect and admiration, praising their stitching and on-time delivery after studying their work.

qa.q: Why is Ritu's proposal a wise move?
qa.a: It learns from a rival's strengths and proposes collaboration where interests align, without giving up competition elsewhere.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see Ritu's email?
qa.a: Lakshmi may be surprised and flattered by the respect, and interested but cautious about working with a competitor.

grounding: The email shows someone who admits a competitor consistently delivers well, respecting and learning from them, and proposing collaboration where interests align.

passage:
April. A big bakery chain opened a shiny outlet two doors down from Minakshi's small bakery in Jayanagar. Their cakes were cheaper. Minakshi couldn't sleep. Her partner, Sangeeta, found her doing sums at 2 a.m.

May. A supplier offered Minakshi cheaper butter "without the paperwork." It would cut costs. She was tempted. Sangeeta said, "We don't cut corners. That's the one thing we have." Minakshi said no.

They talked to their regulars instead. The regulars didn't care about the cheapest cake. They cared about the eggless birthday cakes Minakshi made to order, and that she remembered every child's name.

June. Minakshi dropped the plain sponges the chain sold cheaper and doubled down on custom eggless cakes. She called her five biggest customers, the schools and the old-age home, and thanked them. She gave her baker a raise so he wouldn't be poached.

By August, orders were up. The chain was still there. Minakshi was sleeping again.

qa.q: What did the supplier offer Minakshi?
qa.a: Cheaper butter "without the paperwork."

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling in April?
qa.a: She felt afraid and anxious about the bigger competitor, unable to sleep.

qa.q: What choices helped Minakshi's bakery survive?
qa.a: Refusing the shady butter deal, focusing on custom eggless cakes, protecting key customers and keeping her baker.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see the supplier's offer?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees it as a shortcut that would betray the bakery's honesty, the one thing they have.

grounding: Over several months, the passage shows a small firm fearing a bigger competitor, focusing on its niche and customers, protecting key staff, and refusing unethical shortcuts.

passage:
"Pranav, you look worried about that big firm moving into your area. Let me tell you about my printing press.

When I, Nandini, was twenty-five, I ran a tiny press in Mysuru with my father's old machines. Then a huge printing company from Bengaluru opened a branch nearby. Faster, cheaper, glossy. I was terrified. I thought we'd close in a year.

One of their salesmen told me I could survive if I 'borrowed' their client list from a man who'd left them. I said no. My stomach hurt for days, but I said no.

Instead, I thought about what we did better. We printed in Kannada beautifully. We did wedding cards with hand-set type. We knew every temple committee by name.

So I focused on those. I visited my twelve biggest customers personally. I kept my two best typesetters by giving them a share of each wedding order.

The big firm is still there, beta. So am I."

qa.q: What did the salesman suggest Nandini do?
qa.a: Borrow their client list from a man who had left the company.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when the big printing company opened nearby?
qa.a: Nandini felt terrified, sure the press would close within a year.

qa.q: What choice in Nandini's story helped the press survive?
qa.a: Refusing the stolen client list, focusing on Kannada printing, wedding cards and temple committees, and protecting key customers and typesetters.

qa.q: How might the twelve biggest customers have seen Nandini's personal visits?
qa.a: They likely felt valued and loyal, since Nandini knew them and came in person.

grounding: An elder recalls fearing a bigger competitor, focusing on niches and relationships, protecting clients and staff, and refusing an unethical shortcut.

passage:
I'm Tanuja. Last year, the promotion to senior analyst went to a colleague who'd been on the team eight months less than me. My reviews were better. The whispered reason: the director "preferred not to promote people who might go on maternity leave." I was a newly married woman.

I felt helpless. It seemed like a wall I couldn't move.

Joseph, a colleague who'd seen my reviews, said, "Write it all down first." So I did: dates, review scores, what was said.

Then I weighed it. I went to HR with my records. They were polite and did nothing. I spoke to a lawyer at a women's legal aid centre, who explained my options honestly: a complaint was possible but would take years and might sour my career there.

I decided not to fight that one in court. Instead, I kept my records, got two strong references, and moved to a firm with a better record on promotions.

Choosing not to fight wasn't giving up. It was choosing where to spend my energy.

qa.q: How much less time had the promoted colleague been on the team?
qa.a: Eight months less than Tanuja.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she heard the whispered reason?
qa.a: She felt helpless and wronged, as if facing a wall she couldn't move.

qa.q: What steps did Tanuja take before deciding?
qa.a: She documented everything, went to HR, and spoke to a legal aid lawyer about her options before choosing where to spend her energy.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Tanuja's situation?
qa.a: Joseph sees it as unfair, having seen her reviews, and supports her by suggesting she document everything.

grounding: The reflective account shows a young woman facing a biased promotion decision, documenting it, seeking allies and formal routes, and deciding which fight she could afford.

passage:
Union representative's note, textile unit, Tuesday

Manjula, a quality checker, came to the union office today. She has been transferred to the night shift with one day's notice, right after she reported that the new machines had faulty guards. She thinks the transfer is punishment. So do I.

She was shaking. "What can I even do? They're the company."

I told her the decision is not as immovable as it feels. We wrote down the dates of her report, the transfer order, and the names of two co-workers who heard her supervisor say she "should learn to keep quiet."

I explained the routes: a union grievance, and if needed a complaint to the labour office. I also said it was her choice how far to go, and that choosing a smaller step is not weakness.

She decided to file the union grievance and see what happens before anything more.

Next step: I will present the grievance at Friday's meeting with management.

Leela, union representative

qa.q: What had Manjula reported before being transferred?
qa.a: That the new machines had faulty guards.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she said "They're the company"?
qa.a: She felt helpless and frightened, shaking at the thought of fighting her employer.

qa.q: What did Leela help Manjula do?
qa.a: Document the dates and witnesses, understand the union and labour office routes, and choose how far to take it.

qa.q: How might the supervisor see Manjula's grievance?
qa.a: The supervisor may be caught off guard, since the transfer was meant to keep her quiet.

grounding: A union representative's note shows a young worker facing an unfair, seemingly immovable decision, documenting it, finding allies and formal routes, and choosing what fight to take on.

passage:
At the Monday review in the Kolkata insurance office, the branch manager blamed Naveen for a lost client file. "Careless," he said, in front of everyone. Naveen went red and said nothing.

Indu knew it wasn't true. The file had gone missing when the manager's own assistant moved the cabinets. She'd seen it.

Her heart pounded. Speaking up could cost her. Silence would cost Naveen more.

After the meeting, she went to Naveen's desk. "I saw the cabinets being moved on Thursday. Do you have the email about the file?"

He did. Together they collected it, plus a message from the assistant confirming the move. Two other colleagues who'd seen it agreed to stand with them.

The next morning, Indu asked the manager for five minutes. She kept her voice calm. "Sir, I think there's been a mix-up about the file. Here's what happened."

The manager read the emails, frowned, and said, "I'll correct the record." Naveen looked at Indu as if she'd handed him a life raft.

qa.q: When did Indu see the cabinets being moved?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling before she spoke to the manager?
qa.a: She felt nervous, her heart pounding, knowing speaking up could cost her.

qa.q: What made Indu's support effective?
qa.a: She gathered facts like the email and the assistant's message, found allies, and spoke to the manager calmly.

qa.q: How does Naveen see Indu's help?
qa.a: Naveen feels deeply grateful, as though she threw him a life raft.

grounding: The passage shows someone who sees a coworker treated unfairly and speaks up with facts and allies despite the risk, instead of staying silent.

passage:
"Anirban, what happened in there?" Mehak asked as he came out of the team lead's cabin.

"She refused my leave. Baba's surgery is on Friday, and she says the project comes first."

"But Suresh got leave for his holiday last month."

"I know." His voice cracked. "I can't lose this job."

Mehak thought for a moment. It was risky to push. But if she said nothing, everyone would learn this was normal.

"Okay. Do you have the leave policy?"

"It's on the intranet."

"Print it. Family medical leave is in there. I'll cover your tasks on Friday, in writing. And I'll ask the two seniors on our team if they'll back the plan too."

"You'd do that?"

"I would."

By evening, they had the policy, a written cover plan signed by three colleagues, and a polite email to HR. The next morning, Anirban's leave was approved. He found a packet of biscuits on his desk with a note: "For the hospital. —M."

qa.q: When was Anirban's father's surgery?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling as she thought about pushing back?
qa.a: She felt uneasy about the risk but determined, not wanting everyone to learn that unfairness was normal.

qa.q: What steps made Mehak's support effective?
qa.a: She used the leave policy, offered written cover for his tasks, got colleagues to back the plan, and emailed HR politely.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel finding the biscuits and note?
qa.a: Anirban would likely feel grateful and less alone as he goes to the hospital.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone supporting a coworker treated unfairly over leave, using facts, allies and formal routes rather than staying silent.

passage:
Chandrika had exactly one hour before the disciplinary meeting. The finance head had accused her of approving a wrong payment, and she was sure she'd been set up to cover someone else's mistake. Her hands were cold. She'd already drafted a resignation letter on her phone.

Then Chinmay, from the next team, knocked on the empty meeting room where she was sitting. "I saw the approval chain. You weren't even copied on the final sign-off. I've printed it."

She stared at him. "Why are you doing this? You could get in trouble."

"Because it's wrong."

In the meeting, Chinmay's printout showed the chain clearly. The finance head backed down. The charge was dropped.

Afterwards Chandrika found him at the tea machine. "Thank you. I was going to quit today."

"Don't," he said, grinning.

She deleted the resignation letter. The next week, when his manager asked who had shared the document, Chandrika said, "I requested it," to keep him clear.

qa.q: What had Chandrika drafted on her phone?
qa.a: A resignation letter.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling before the meeting?
qa.a: She felt frightened and hopeless, her hands cold, ready to give up and quit.

qa.q: How did Chandrika respond to Chinmay's support?
qa.a: She thanked him, stayed in her job, and protected him from consequences by saying she had requested the document.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see standing by Chandrika?
qa.a: Chinmay sees it simply as the right thing to do because the accusation was wrong, despite the risk.

grounding: Under the pressure of a disciplinary meeting, the passage shows someone treated unfairly receiving a coworker's support, thanking him, protecting him from consequences and not giving up.

passage:
Karthik had been passed over for the Singapore posting even though he'd built the client relationship. His manager gave it to someone from his own hometown and told Karthik he "wasn't the right fit."

Karthik stopped talking in meetings. He started applying for jobs elsewhere.

Sabina, a senior analyst on another team, noticed. She came to his desk with a spreadsheet. "I pulled the client emails. They mention you by name twelve times. They asked for you. I've sent it to HR, and I'll say it in the review panel too."

Karthik didn't know what to say. "You don't have to."

"I know. I want to."

The panel reversed the decision a week later.

That evening, Karthik took Sabina for dinner at the Chettinad place she loved. "I was about to give up," he said. "I won't forget this."

When she later faced a tough review of her own, he was the first to write her a reference.

qa.q: How many times did the client emails mention Karthik by name?
qa.a: Twelve times.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling after being passed over?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and hurt, so much that he stopped talking in meetings and started applying elsewhere.

qa.q: How did Karthik show gratitude to Sabina?
qa.a: He thanked her over dinner, promised not to forget, and later wrote her a reference when she needed support.

qa.q: How does Sabina see her decision to help?
qa.a: Sabina sees it as something she wants to do, not an obligation, because the facts showed Karthik had been wronged.

grounding: The passage shows someone treated unfairly who receives a coworker's support, thanks her, remembers the debt and repays it, and does not give up.

passage:
Monday. Nirmala woke at five, lit the lamp before the small Ganesha in her Thane kitchen, and felt a flood of thanks: for the job she almost didn't get, for surviving last year's typhoid, for her mother's voice on the phone. She sat there longer than usual.

Wednesday. At the office, the new cleaner, Ayesha, dropped a tray of cups. Everyone sighed loudly. Nirmala remembered her own first week, when someone had helped her. She knelt and picked up pieces with Ayesha, and asked her name.

Saturday. Nirmala did her usual puja, then took the leftover prasad and a packet of new notebooks to Ayesha's daughter, who was starting school. Ayesha cried a little and pressed her hand.

On the train home, Nirmala thought her prayer felt more complete that week than it had in years. Thanking God on Monday, she realised, only half counted until she thanked people too.

qa.q: What did Nirmala take to Ayesha's daughter?
qa.a: Leftover prasad and a packet of new notebooks.

passage:
"Rajni, you asked why I always give the first plate at the gurdwara langar to the sweepers. Let me tell you.

When I, Divyansh, was twenty-five, I lost my job in the mill closure and my wife was expecting. I prayed every night in fear. Then a neighbour got me work at a printing press. The baby came safe. I felt such thanks to God I could have burst.

I started going to the gurdwara every morning, reciting, bowing. I felt very holy.

But one day an old granthi watched me walk straight past the sweeper who'd cleaned the steps, without a word, and said, 'Your prayer is loud, son. Your eyes are closed.'

It stung. He was right. I'd thanked God and forgotten the people God had sent.

So I started small. Tea for the sweeper. Thanking the neighbour properly. Serving langar every Sunday.

Gratitude that stays inside the prayer hall is only half a prayer, beta."

qa.q: What work did the neighbour get Divyansh?
qa.a: Work at a printing press.

qa.q: What did Divyansh feel when the old granthi spoke to him?
qa.a: He felt stung and ashamed, realising he had forgotten the people around him.

qa.q: Which choice in Divyansh's story turned devotion into kindness?
qa.a: Starting small with tea for the sweeper, thanking the neighbour properly and serving langar every Sunday.

qa.q: How might the sweeper have seen young Divyansh before the change?
qa.a: The sweeper may have felt invisible and unappreciated, watching him walk past without a word.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling deep thanks to God for hard times survived, and learning that devotion without kindness to others is incomplete.
